monastic

/muh-NAS-tik/ - rhymes with elastic · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Monastic means austerely simple and disciplined, like the life of monks.

The submarine crew kept a nearly monastic existence on patrol — narrow bunks, fixed watches, and months of enforced quiet.

Example

Keepers in the old lighthouse service lived monastic lives: two men on a bare rock, a logbook, a Bible, and a clockwork routine of watches that never varied by a minute. Visitors from the mainland found the bare rooms grim; the keepers themselves spoke of the calm that came from owning nothing and missing nothing.

Monastic says more than spartan: spartan describes only the bare furnishings, but monastic wraps the whole way of living — the fixed hours, the silence, the withdrawal from ordinary appetites — into one word. A room can be spartan; a life is monastic.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

ascetic: An ascetic life gives up comforts on principle — plain food, hard beds, few possessions — usually in the name of spiritual or personal discipline. Monastic includes that self-denial but goes wider, naming a whole rule-governed way of living: fixed hours, silence, routine. Ascetic tells you what someone refuses; monastic tells you the regimen they follow.

disciplined: Disciplined means governed by rules and self-control — a disciplined athlete trains on schedule whatever the weather. The word says nothing about plainness or withdrawal, and a disciplined life can be full of luxuries. Monastic requires both halves at once: the discipline and the bareness, appetites refused along with hours fixed.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

indulgent: freely giving in to comfort and appetite

extravagant: spending and enjoying far beyond need

Where it sits · how much of life the plainness governs

simple → spartan → monastic → cloistered

simple vs. monastic: A simple room just lacks clutter; monastic demands far more — bareness chosen on purpose and a rule to live by.

spartan vs. monastic: Spartan strips the comforts from the room; monastic goes further and strips them from the whole schedule, the meals, the company.

cloistered vs. monastic: Cloistered outdoes even monastic: a monastic coder still walks to the office, while a cloistered nun never passes the convent wall.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — monast: living alone (Greek monos, alone)

Suffix — -ic: relating to, like

Put it together: Monast (living alone) + -ic (like) = like one who lives alone. Greek monos means alone; a monasterion was literally a place for living alone, and monastic carried the monks' whole package — solitude, plainness, fixed hours — into English as a single adjective.

Use the root in a new word: monologue: The play opens with a ten-minute monologue delivered to an empty stage.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Monastic borrows the monks' whole regimen — bare rooms, fixed hours, appetites refused — and needs no actual religion to work. Use spartan when only the furnishings are bare, and reach for this unit's seclusion when the point is being hidden from people rather than living by a rule; a monastic training camp can be crowded.
